This comment is regarding the approval for to Dancing Moose school. Before the building of a school, or
any other large building is considered in the Thanksgiving point area, the traffic problem at 2150 N and
2300 W must be addressed. As a city resident who lives in this area I want to put my voice with all the
others who live in this area. Getting out of our neighborhood during peak traffic times is nearly

impossible. With the extension of Triumph Blvd. over I-15 traffic has only increased making it difficult to
get out not only during evening rush hour but as early at three in the afternoon. This impacts the daily
life of everyone in this neighborhood making it difficult to pick kids up from school, get to necessary
appointment on time, attend to recreational activities, and even attend city council meetings. There
have been many close calls at this intersection as well as multiple accidents due to the high traffic
volume flowing by our neighborhood and the refusal of many drivers to leave the intersection clear.
Until the city sees fit to find a solution to the traffic at this intersection then further development in the
Thanksgiving point area should be off the table.

While a full traffic light may not be feasible due to the close distance to 2100 N, perhaps a light that runs
in conjunction with the 2100 N light could be used. This light would turn red for the 2300 W traffic
several seconds before the 2100 N light turns red, thus allowing cars to safely travel out of both sides of
2150N. The intersection of 2100 N and 2300 W should also be treated more fairly for all directions of
traffic flow. The light going south on 2300 W is very short causing further back up along this road while
traffic on 2100 N barely starts to see a build up with its long light cycles.

Some may argue that if this is a problem then we should just move. Even if this was an option, which for
many of us it isn’t. Moving just takes the problem from the current residents and transfers it to the new
ones. It is time for the city to do its due duty in taking care of all its citizens. Our neighborhood cannot
continue to be ignored. Please fix this problem instead of continuing to ignore it and allowing it to get
worse.

Thank you for your time.
Anya Oakes
Lehi city resident

The problem with building another school ( or any other building) in the Thanksgiving point area is that
the traffic on triumph bulvd is already too much. We cannot get out of our neighborhood in the
mornings or evenings. Drivers are not keeping the intersection clear when the light at 2100 turns red. If
the city would install a traffic light at 2300 it would help. I know it is close to the one at 2100, but it just
needs to follow the one at 2100 and turn green with a small delay so drivers on both sides of 2100 have
a chance to turn.

Until the traffic has been mitigated the city should not approve any other projects in the area.
Tanner

A couple thoughts:

Thank you city council for your attention. I'm writing today as a resident of Cranberry Farms who built
here in 2007.

RE: #4 the Montessori school:

1. I’ve never really heard anyone speak badly about Montessori, ever.
I think it’d be a good asset to the community and the office park is a reasonable location.

However…

1. Months ago, the mayor put a hold on new building in the park pending traffic issues, etc. This has
surely frustrated Stack, one of the main developers, and also the folks who wanted to park a thousand

foot long parking garage on the northern side of the Pointe Meadows fence. My totally uninformed
suspicion is that if the Moose group is given the go-ahead, Stack will sue and likely win because they
don’t get the same treatment. Our tax dollars will pay for this fight.

What will the city say when those proposed 1,800 - 3,600 residential units, rumored to be built in the
office park as well, are pushed through quickly?

2. This appeared on the agenda MONDAY afternoon March 30. As of Tuesday morning, there are no
maps available. Council, I don’t feel like you can make good decisions with so little time available for
research and discussion. This feels rushed, disorganized and less than transparent. Is this fair to you and
your constituents? What precedent is being set tonight? Can this be tabled and researched more?

3. Adding any traffic at all ruins our currently failing intersection at 2150 N 2300 W even more. If the city
plans to allow more development, we, the residents, deserve help with traffic. We live here. Everyone
else just commutes past the driveways and side streets we're stuck in. We’ve asked for help for years
with zero action. We're tired of 'studies being considered' and 'let's see what staff can do'
and 'well UDOT is in charge as well.'

Please, do something. Throw us a bone. Paint 'do not block intersection' on the road in offensively large
letters. Add large flashing signs to warn cars as they approach. Park a spare officer or two nearby to
harass the selfish, oblivious commuters who clog these roads and fail to yield. The city could make a
fortune selling speeding tickets to those heading south under the train bridge during the day. Yes,
there's currently one single sign. No, it's not at all obvious in heavy traffic unless you're driving
southbound in the far west lane.

Please keep this in mind as well: regardless of how many emails you may hear today, every resident of

our concerns have been ignored and glossed over for years. Every time a new building is approved, we're
reminded that established homes and families are less important than keeping business moving.

Our kids have to be driven across the neighborhood to visit their friends. It's wasteful and embarrassing
to need a car for a playdate three blocks away. Many, many of my personal friends have moved away
due to traffic frustrations. We've personally considered it more than once. Please be responsible as you
consider allowing future growth.

Thanks for your time.

John & Shiloam Chapman

subject: Written public comment (published in minutes)
topic: Dancing Moose Montessori daycare / Thanksgiving Point Area Plan
comment:
Dear City Council,

I wanted to reach out in support of Dancing Moose’s request on Tuesday’s City Council Agenda. Our
daughter Lia attended Preschool at Dancing Moose – we adopted her from China & were concerned she
was behind, so I drove her to their Campus in South Jordan so she could attend. As a Dancing Moose
alumni, I can share that they run a world-class program that really enriches kids and flexes their schedule
to support the needs of working families. Lehi doesn’t have a resource like this – and Dancing Moose
will truly fill a critical gap for families in Thanksgiving Point area, workers who come to Thanksgiving
Point, and businesses in the area trying to help employees strike a positive work/life balance.

Here are the key issues that I’ve seen flagged with respect to the project:

    1. Traffic Impact: Will Dancing Moose negatively impact AM traffic in Thanksgiving Point? The
       Mayor flagged this issue for them & they’ve responded with an enhanced traffic study…and a
       proposal to stagger their AM class start times to stretch out their arrival windows and minimize
       traffic impact. Their current staggered-start plan will a minimal impact on area traffic in the
       mornings & no appreciable impact on evening traffic.
    2. Erode Recreational/Open Space in TGP: Will DM’s 1.5 acre campus bring TGP below the 60%
       threshold for Recreational Use Property required by the TGP area plan. Answer – absolutely not,
       according to Mike Washburn at TGP… “not even close.”
    3. Align with Thanksgiving Point’s Technology Architectural Standard: Dancing Moose has
       updated their building elevations & they are absolutely beautiful – so main entrance is over 50%
       glass & exceeds the standard. The class rooms will sit behind iron fencing/hedges to protect
       student privacy and provide security, so the other parts of the building shouldn’t need to adhere

to the Technology Architectural Standard standard. (TGP has said this updated design will pass

       Thanksgiving Point: Some have expressed concern that making an exception for Dancing Moose
       to build their campus would create a back door for other developers wanting to start additional

subject: Written public comment (published in minutes)
topic: Dancing Moose Montessori daycare / Thanksgiving Point Area Plan
comment:
4811 N. Aspen Wood Loop

Lehi, UT 84043

Council Members and city officials,

I certainly wish we were able to meet to discuss the Dancing Moose Montessori school.

I’ve been asking for the agendas to be sent or posted as soon as they were available. I
am noticing that this has come late to the meeting, where maps and resources are not
instituted in the docket. My question is, how can council members discuss an item
where not all information has been submitted or processed? It seems that this is a
rushed issue. Is it something you think you can pass quickly just because no one is
present at the meeting or you won’t have large community comments? It almost feels as
if it’s expected to be a simple, quick vote. And it shouldn’t be.

While on the whole, I have no quarrels with the school and feel that it could serve it’s
community and purpose well, I do have a major issue with the location and timing of the
item. I know that Mayor Johnson instituted a moratorium on builds within Thanksgiving
Point’s office park. This would mean that if you allow this, you are making an exception,
allowing a build to move forward. I also know that Stacks has come in and asked for
more units to be built, but was told no until the traffic is addressed and/or fixed. If you
allow the school to be built, who’s to say Stack and other developers won’t come at you
and say, wait a minute…and then you’ll have a lawsuit on your hands, that will cause
taxpayers to pay for the lawsuit.

Stop. Think about the ramifications you are potentially creating. Will you be setting the
city up for such outcomes? If so, do not vote yes. Do not allow the build/plans to
progress.

Now think about the Ashton’s and Thanksgiving Point. I’ve grown up with the Ashton’s
and extended family my high school years and throughout. Our family has purchased
memberships over the course of the many years we have lived in Lehi. We know they
do great things for the community. But if they are asking for the build to happen to
create gains or to help them, if they are in a pinch, then why is the city trying to bail
them out? They’re a non-profit organization. They also shot themselves in the foot long
ago, by not creating a proper plan that suited their land and company, as soon as they
moved it from just a gardens to so much more. They did not have the foresight to
accommodate the traffic that would come — and I honestly believe they knew people
would come. That was their goal. They built on property out in the middle of nowhere,
without secondary, third, or fourth exits and honestly, it was something that didn’t meet
the growth of the city.

I know that sounds harsh. I’m not trying to put a bad light on Thanksgiving Point or the
Ashton’s because they have done a great deal to bring consumers, homeowners,
businesses, etc. into our city. And they have every right to build on their property(ies)
EXCEPT with the moratorium that has been put in place. I think if they were to build,
there must be a proper updated area model that specifically addresses or accounts for
the businesses (population per site) plus traffic that comes and goes through the
community. And an area plan must meet the necessary bylaws and rules the city must
follow. No exceptions. No pauses. No, lets just see how this goes… It must be an

approved area plan by all board members, with the knowledge that this city will continue
to grow at a rapid pace.

A few months ago, I noticed a few city engineers on site at the corner of 2100 N and
2300 W. It seemed odd, because I hadn’t seen it on an agenda or heard about it from
the last minutes, so I reached out to a few council members and asked what was up. In
their response, it was something that would be addressed at some future meeting. That
didn’t sit well so I’ve been watching, waiting and making calls. I’ve tried to learn more
and from conversations and what has been placed on agenda items, it’s apparent that
the business park has companies wanting to build as soon as possible.

I know that if you allow the school to open, Stack will file a lawsuit. If they win, they’ve
asked to build a 3000 unit within the office park. If that happens, the traffic will
dramatically increase. Rumor is that they would offer to widen the roads, which would
require homes to be purchased. That then means an entire community - not a few
homes- would be directly effected, ours included. Instead of chance crossing the four/
five lane roads, it will be more and you’ll force us out. This has nothing to do with
representing a community or citizens, but a business. Which makes it feel more about
the bottom line dollar then the folks who ask for help living in a live-able area.

We have lived in Cranberry Farms since February/March of 2007. We’ve watched our
quiet neighborhood over the years turn into one of the busiest sections of the city. We
have been asking for a break for years to help the Cranberry Farms, Thanksgiving
Village, Point Meadows areas by having a light at 2150 N 2300 W as the traffic
increases exponentially. We’ve suggested paint in big bold letters “DO NOT BLOCK”
with areas that it has shown successful in Utah, but still nothing. We’ve asked for
flashing lights. Nothing. We’ve asked for police officers to come ticket citizens that
stupidly block this intersection and don’t allow residence — not business people —
residence a chance to get out of their neighborhood and homes. Still nothing.

Ever since our communities came together to voice our concern about the Family
Search building going in (changing resort to business and traffic increase) and another
road extension (I can’t remember the amount but millions to build a second road north/
south, the concerns weren’t fully addressed and the money left, that it left a strained
relationship with Mayor Johnson and this area of community; like we’re just a bunch of
annoying citizens that don’t want growth. Well, we do, but we are truly stuck and need
help. We need the city to hear our concerns. None who sit on the council today live
currently in the community. Katie Koivisto once lived in the pointe meadows community
and can probably attest to the struggles residence have here.

We’ve gone to counsel meetings. We’ve approached this issue time and time again.
We are sick of “studies” that go nowhere. We’re sick of broken promises that you’ll
maintain the infrastructure, improve the commute and traffic. We’re tired of not being
heard. Your job as council members is to lead the citizens and it’s community and now
you’re giving us a meeting where we can’t even have public comment? Will you not
even read this aloud and allow the recorder to state our frustrations?

Sometimes I’ve attended counsel meetings and have heard public comment that gives
me a deeper appreciation for dialogue and understanding. By stating we have received
emails, and have you read them — then make a vote is not transparent. It is not
allowing the public to be heard. I want to know what is happening in other areas, not
just by reading an agenda and listening to the minutes. I can’t know what’s happening
face to face with social distancing so I feel as if my information (and everyone) should
be approached as if we were there in person to make our comments heard.

But if you make the exception and allow the build to happen, then make the exception
and give us a light. I mean, after all, it’s just this one exception.

subject: Please grant an exception for Dancing Moose Montessori School
topic: Dancing Moose Montessori daycare / Thanksgiving Point Area Plan
comment:
Dear Mayor Johnson, Distinguished Council Members, and Lehi City Planners,

I write today to provide my perspective on why Lehi City Council should make an exception for
Dancing Moose Montessori School to the current construction moratorium. But for
#socialdistancing, I would be front and center at tomorrow’s originally-planned city council
meeting.

I have two daughters (2 and 4-years-old). My husband and I live in Murray and both work at
Adobe. As full-time working parents, we had to face the reality of finding childcare for our girls.
As any parent knows, making that decision is hard, but even harder than that is finding care that
justifies the sacrifice. I spent months visiting day cares and preschools, and interviewing
potential nannies. I had all but given up and decided to put my legal career on hold to be at
home with my girls. Then, I heard about Dancing Moose. As soon as I walked in the doors, my
very anxious/worried mama heart was at peace.

My 4-year-old has attended DM for 3 years and will start kindergarten next year. My 2-year-old
is finishing her first year of (pre) preschool. Every day I drop off my girls, my mind is at ease and
warmed with gratitude for the school, the curriculum, the teachers, the directors, and the staff.

My girls are fed healthy, whole food meals for lunch and snack, they are loved beyond belief,
and the security measures the school has in place (bio-authentication and locked doors, active
shooter preparation, panic buttons immediately connecting police and first responders,
pandemic planning, etc.) are invaluable. The school is
clean… So. Unbelievably. Clean. Quite frankly, I don’t know how they do it! I often profess,
as I’m certain other parents of DM children do, that my children are their teachers’ favorite. And
all of the parents that profess that would be telling the truth. The teachers know my girls. They
take proactive steps to get to know the parents and older/younger siblings. The staff know all
the kids’ names AND the parents’ names. It’s remarkable. The Dancing Moose family is my
family and I’m very protective of my family members.

As Lehi City continues to grow, particularly with families moving from out of town to Silicon
Slopes, top notch education is a priority. People with young children put that as their top priority
when determining where to purchase a home. Several of my Adobe colleagues have children
that also attend DM. They all, categorically, will say they are beyond grateful for DM. The
flexible drop off and pick up times are a godsend for working parents. Because of the staggered
drop off and pick up times, there is never traffic. In fact, I almost always pull straight in to “front
row joe” parking, as my daughters refer to it. It is so relieving to know that my kids won’t be put
in a position where they have to wait for their mom or dad to finally drive up after s/he has been
waiting in a line of cars, or that they will be in any danger of walking in a parking lot that is
chaotic. I’ve picked my niece and nephew up from their charter school and, well, I feel frustrated
and anxious the entire time. Not the case at DM.

I think it is important to let you know the skills DM has fostered in my children. My 2-year-old
dresses herself, puts shoes on by herself, is nearly potty trained because DM helps train her,
and knows letters/numbers/colors and the solar system. My four-year-old does the dishes,
brushes her teeth better than most adults, speaks Spanish, and refuses help most of the time.

But most importantly, my girls are learning the value of kindness, mindfulness, gratitude,
creative thinking, cooperation, and confidence.

As Lehi grows into a tech mecca, we need early education schools that focus on 21st century
skills more than ever. Parents demand it. Whether parents are entrepreneurs, tech CEOs,
athletes, teachers, or like every other parent wanting to raise competent, out-of-the-box-
thinking, kind kids….they all want the best. That is Dancing Moose. You have an opportunity to
take the lead in providing early education options for your constituents. The ROI in early
childhood education for communities can’t be overstated.

Please. Invest in the City. Invest in the future. Invest in the community. Make an exception for
Dancing Moose.

I am a parent who lives in Northern Utah County who is desperately wishing that we had
Montessori options for my children. I've lived in Utah County for 7 years, and have
looked multiple times for options for my two children. As there is only one, and I can't
seem to get off their waiting list, I drive 30 minutes into Salt Lake County to drop my

were in your schools than those in other counties because you didn't provide the
option?

subject: Written public comment (published in minutes)
topic: Dancing Moose Montessori daycare / Thanksgiving Point Area Plan
comment:
Dear Mayor Johnson and Lehi City Council Members,
        My name is Spencer Black and I am a husband of one of the teachers and the father of one of
the students who hope to teach at and attend the Dancing Moose Montessori School

at Thanksgiving Point in Lehi. I’m writing because I believe that the Dancing Moose Montessori School is
just what the community, Lehi city, and Thanksgiving Point needs.
        It is not just another school, Montessori is different and amazing. The style of learning is
innovative, natural, hands on learning at a student’s own pace, and if you haven’t researched
Montessori learning, please do so you can see the beauty of it. It really makes learning fun and
exciting. I took our little family to Thanksgiving Point last month to the butterfly museum and when I
saw the style of learning through curiosity and exploration I thought, this is exactly the same as Dancing
Moose. The learning experience of Dancing Moose at that location would be incredible if combined
with the hands on, curiosity and exploration of Thanksgiving Point. I think we would all hope to have
that kind of fun, quality education for all our children. Especially for all those parents who work very
near Thanksgiving point and are searching for any childcare remotely close.
         The design of this new school would be wonderful for that area. Even the designs of the
classrooms with less metal and plastic and more wood give a peaceful feel to learning. Natural light is
wonderful in the classroom, but requiring 40% of the glass on the front of the building is too much. My
son started attending when he was 18 months and now that he is three, he still needs a nap every
day. It is so hard and expensive to close the windows for nap time if there is too much glass. I’ve seen
renderings of the proposed building and it is a single story, low profile building that is beautiful, but
requiring that much glass is not practical. It will still add to the beauty of the city and area. Besides the
privacy and protection of students, too big of windows become distractions from learning. Dancing
Moose is not a commercial building and shouldn’t have to follow the same expectations since it can still
be a beautiful addition to the community.
         I realize that traffic is a big concern when adding a school to an area that already has some
traffic problems. I have never seen a traffic problem during drop off or pick up time at the Dancing
Moose school in South Jordan. The system is brilliant. They have different programs and classes that
kids can participate in before and after school so there is a wide range of times to drop off kids based on
parent’s work schedules. This flexibility is not only convenient for the parents in the community but is
the perfect system to accommodate the problem of irregular traffic delays because of their staggered
drop off times. The system that Dancing Moose has for drop off and pick up definitely won’t make
traffic worse, and it might actually help traffic by getting cars off the roads by shorting the distance
between the parent’s work and the closest school where they drop off their kids.
        Dancing Moose Montessori School would be such a great contribution to the city. Not only is
the quality of education amazing, but the teachers and faculty are INCREDIBLE. I have friends from my
work who are raising kids and when we talk about education, I am surprised how many of them have
looked for quality learning and have looked for Montessori. When I tell them my wife teaches
Montessori and has a master’s degree in it, they always want to know more and wish there were more
Montessori schools available. I have a close friend who is employed at Workfront in Lehi and would love
to have more childcare options available in that area. There is a need and a hope for this school from
many in the community. We hope and pray that as a city council you can waive these construction
setbacks for this amazing project.
Thank you for taking the time to read this letter and I hope you take into consideration the many quality
characteristics of Dancing Moose Montessori School and the wonderful asset it would be to the Lehi
community.

subject: Written public comment (published in minutes)

comment:
Dear Mayor Mark Johnson, the Lehi City Council, and Lehi City Planners,

It has come to my attention that the city of Lehi has enacted a construction
moratorium on the construction of Dancing Moose’s Lehi campus.

As a Lehi resident and parent of two young sons who currently attend Dancing
Moose in South Jordan, I am very disappointed that Lehi City has halted the
project.

Please consider the following reasons why lifting the construction moratorium will
be in the absolute best interest of Lehi City.

   1. Dancing Moose is a perfect fit for Lehi’s innovative and technological
      landscape. Rather than emphasizing memorization and arbitrary academic
      feats, Dancing Moose is focused on teaching young children the love of
      learning. The teachers and staff act as guides in the classroom to help
      children learn by following the child’s interests. My boys are excelling

subject: Written public comment (published in minutes)
topic: Dancing Moose Montessori daycare / Thanksgiving Point Area Plan
comment:
Dear Mayor Johnson and Lehi City Council Members,

My name is Kiley Black and I am a teacher and a parent at the Dancing Moose River Park location in
South Jordan, UT. I live in Pleasant Grove, UT and have been teaching at Dancing Moose Montessori
School for the last two years.

The two current Dancing Moose Montessori Schools are both beautiful schools, inside and out. The
outside of the schools are aesthetically pleasing, relying on the natural colors that are typically found in
the beautiful Utah valleys and mountains. The school relies on a large amount of natural light to light the
school. Even on rainy days, the sun shines through the roof into the hallways, providing a peaceful and
natural atmosphere to the school. I understand that the proposition for the new school in Lehi is zoned
for a commercial building that would typically require 40% glass on the front, however, as a school,
placing 40% glass on the front could cause an invasion of privacy for the students and increase
distractions in a child's natural learning. Both as a teacher and a parent, I would be uncomfortable
knowing that my child's school was mostly windows on the front. Knowing that the current Dancing
Moose Montessori School's both have immense amounts of light and natural beauty, requiring a school
to meet the same expectations as a commercial building may not be appropriate.

Outside of the windows, there are so many wonderful features that Dancing Moose Montessori School
has. It is a high quality education for early childhood in that children are able to learn at their own pace
with the direction of not one, but two or three teachers per classroom. The lower student ratios allow
children to receive the education that best fits their needs while providing opportunities to learn
through critical thinking, discovery, hands-on learning, and creativity. The education that is provided by
Dancing Moose is an opportunity to help inspire a love of learning. Having a new school built in such
close proximity to Thanksgiving Point would allow students to collaborate with the hands-on learning
and exploratory learning that Thanksgiving Point provides to the community. Children learn through
exploration! Dancing Moose Montessori School does a wonderful job of providing that for their
students, but the added benefit of being so close to the various museums and learning facilities of
Thanksgiving Point would be an experience of a lifetime for the students that attend the school.

Dancing Moose would be a wonderful addition to the Lehi community, especially at the location of
Thanksgiving Point. The design of Dancing Moose Montessori School is one such that children are able to
come to school earlier than the normal start time and stay later than the normal end time. This is in the
design that many parents are both working parents. As children are able to come early and stay late and
participate in programs such as STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, Math), music classes,
cooking classes, and many other after school programs, parents are able to continue working with the
assurance that their child(ren) are in a safe place, without needing to coordinate picking up or dropping
off children with family, friends, or other "daycare" systems during a typical 9-5 work schedule. With the
design of the staggered drop-off and pick-up system at the school, there is very rarely, if ever, a large
influx of cars or drivers all at one time, such that you would normally see in a "drop-off line" at typical
public and many charter schools. Parents are expected to park and bring their children into the school in
order to prevent traffic standstills or lines in the streets in front of the schools. The flow of traffic is
coordinated, systematic, and very well staggered throughout the morning. As such, it would most likely
not create any significant change to the traffic pattern.

Dancing Moose Montessori School not only provides quality early childhood education (typically defined
as preschool through third grade), but also quality learning to our youngest and earliest learners, 18
months through 3 years old. Our toddler program is not a daycare. It is a school learning environment. I

can attest to the quality of the toddler program because my son went through it. He participated in
circle times where he received short lessons and discussions, learning about topics such as letter sounds,
animals of the world, and social and life skills. Dancing Moose Montessori School is not a daycare, it is a
quality education for all ages that attend.

The moment I walked into the school, I immediately felt a sense of peace and calm. The atmosphere is
inviting. The children are happy. The teachers and staff are happy and you can tell they love their jobs.
The entire environment is inviting. The only downside for me was the commute. However, even though I
live in Pleasant Grove, I fell in love with the school and the entire faculty and administration. I make the
commute because I can tell that there is a difference at Dancing Moose Montessori School than any
other school I've ever taught in. In addition, as a teacher and as a parent at Dancing Moose Montessori
School, I am able to feel at ease knowing my child is receiving a quality education. And if he needs me, I
am a quick walk away. Dancing Moose Montessori School cares for their teachers. They care for their
students and the students' families. They care for their community. I look forward to the opportunity to
continue doing what I love at a school I love with a significantly shorter commute, ensuring that I can
also spend more quality time with my family, instead of driving farther.

Thank you for taking the time to read this letter and I hope you take into consideration the many quality
characteristics of Dancing Moose Montessori School and the wonderful asset it would be to the Lehi
community.

425 W 3472 N

Lehi City Council (and Planning Commission):

My family residence is 3459 N 350 W in Lehi. A substantial portion of my backyard abuts the plot
(approx 425 W Bull River Road) that is under consideration for a potential zoning change from
Residential to Commercial. I have a significant interest in the develop of the land that runs contiguous
to my property.

moved in, we had a great view of Lone Peak. However, the commercial storage facility (that was built

the entire storage facility plot to match the topographical elevation of the power sub-station farther to

bringing in dirt to match the northeast elevation was a 22-ft high cinder-block wall, with about 12 feet of
dirt packed behind it (not to mention that the storage facility is graded so that there is a water collection
pond that fills up with several feet deep of water right behind that wall) that forms the border fence
along a portion of my backyard (see the picture of my wife and daughters attached/below). If the
unsightly wall was ever to break (for any reason - earthquakes included), my entire home would be
flooded with a deluge of water. The saying “good fences make good neighbors” is typically accurate, but
when the fence is 22 feet high, most neighbors (my family included) feel that the wall-building (for a
commercial facility) was taken to the extreme.

I share this because if the residential lot in question is re-zoned commercial, my backyard view will look
like a prison fortress. In particular, if the topography continues to be matched with Bull River Road,
which for commercial-purposes makes the most sense for vehicular access, I estimate the wall on the far
end of my back yard will be close to 28-feet tall. That does not make for a good backyard view - nor
does it comport with the General Plan for having a good transition from residential to commercial land
use. Rather, the transition between commercial and residential would be about as blunt and grotesque
as it possibly could be.

The power sub-station and the storage facility that are east of the lot in question do not generate a
substantial amount of vehicular traffic. However, once the plot in question is zoned commercial,
whether a massive day care facility is built upon it or not, whatever does end-up getting built there in
the future could have an unsustainable/dangerous amount of associative vehicular traffic. With
particular regard to the day care facility proposal, there is absolutely no way Bull River Road, which is
lined with residential houses on one side and bounded by the Murdock Trail on the other, could safely
support the traffic - most of which will likely come from the west, where many of the Silicon Slopes
employees will be coming when the drop-off/pick-up their children. The intersection of Bull River Road
and 1200 West is very dangerous already, because vehicles turning south onto 1200 West off Highway
92 accelerate very quickly down the hill. As a consequence, it is very difficult to pull out of Bull River

Road and turn south onto 1200 W safely, without having to gun the car and accelerate as quickly as
possible. Crossing 1200 West directly is very difficult. Additionally, when turning east off of 1200 West
onto Bull River road, there is isn’t much room for the cars bearing down behind you to get around you
while you wait to safely make your turn, and you feel like you are going to get plowed into from the
back. That intersection (Bull River Road and 1200 West) barely/frightfully sustains current traffic load
and simply will not be able to sustain commercial traffic associated with the plot at issue.

There has been talk of re-zoning the plot at issue to a residential/commercial designation (with the
correlative restrictions on commercial use). I would prefer such a re-zoning over a change completely to
commercial, if that is what has to occur. Nevertheless, based on the topography of the land, the
vehicular capacity of Bull River Road, and the constructs of the General Plan, it is my understanding that
the plot at issue should remain zoned Residential. The storage facility already creates a stark
commercial contrast between my residential property (see the massive backyard fence), and if further
commercial development were to occur, the juxtaposition would stand in contrast to the very reasons
for setting-forth and abiding by the General Plan.

Were the property to remain Residential, there could likely be between 1 and 4 subdivided lots that
could be developed for residential homes. Perry Homes (the current owner of the property) could make
a substantial amount of money building 1-4 homes on that land; and those 1-4 homes would perfectly
match the residential nature of the other homes bordering Bull River Road all the way to 1200
West. Moreover, vehicular traffic associated with 1-4 residential homes would not over-burden Bull
River Road like a commercial facility would.

I hope this additional information is helpful as the Planning Commission and City Council considered
whether to re-zone the plot at issue.

Very truly yours,

Jonathan Madsen

workforce.
